speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: This conversation with Ruth Olson and Margaret Olson took place at their home in Deary on June 16th, 1976. The interviewer was Sam Schrager.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: And was crewing up on the homes that are crossed and we were living there. But it was because of Uncle Will's that they came last.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How was that? Because he was already here?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Well, they were here. They were established there. I mean, they were, he had a store there at Elmer. And he and, I thought it was a wonderful country, of course. And he wrote letters like they all do in the local country for us. And the folks decided they would, and mom spoke by mother's,

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: mother and father wanted to come. They didn't come right at that time. They came in the middle of the house.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: But when did Uncle Charlie come?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I don't know.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I can't remember what you were saying.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Were you born by that time?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Yes.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I was just a baby when he came out.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I was born in 1906.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I was born on Homestead.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: They were living out there. And then that little later in the year they were ordered out during that 1910 fire. So they moved off in Homestead and didn't return. They traded a dolphin and moved in here in February of the next year.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: There were a lot of people who had Homesteads right at that time in that country weren't there.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Well, I think that was a lot what was settling this free land, or I mean this land that they could get. And that's what brought them. When you think of the early people, most of them Homesteaded land in here. Mrs. Smith's folks, I imagine they did. The Berklins found their own Bear Creek. And now my sisters, well, the Reuben's folks Homesteaded. The Virginia Bar Arches folks did. They all Homesteaded.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: The Millman's Homesteaded, like where were they? I was thinking that around people that were Homesteading around that area, around Helmer, that was kind of almost right about the edge of where you could farm, wasn't it?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: At least that's the idea that I've had. It was almost, it was pretty much timber that, I mean it's still large of timber, like where you're.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Well, and right, I mean when they came, of course, a lot of this was timber planting that they cleared, I don't know. They're still clearing on some of this. Well, these homesteads around here were timber too. Well, that's why I mean right around here, you know.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Were a lot of those sold to potlatch?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I think so. I think the bottom of them were.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You had that old, in the Lantau County, that the most they had, that shows all the land and the, is that?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Well, that atlas that came out on there. It's at home, that you know, it shows. Now, I know we had some grass from that. The potlatch were one of the, the one woman is from Potlatch and her sisters are scattered out, but they were up here and they were trying to ask us if we could, if we had any idea where their father's homestead was. And we said, well, we didn't know, and so we went out to Arthur Burke and he told us that it was, not by the old city dump.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: So we'd forgotten about there being another dump farther to the south and west a little bit, is it?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: South East, yeah, that way. West, it's west of the dump now.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: And we forgot about that and so we told them that it was by the dump there and then later someone said, oh don't you remember that one?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: And we did recall after they told us just where it was, we did recall there was a dump in a previous place.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: And, oh, when you think of some of them, of course, a lot of them moved away, the Andersons and a lot of the Petercings, the Talcans, Linda Clovers. There was a person that you ought to talk to.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you know Mike Clover down here?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: He doesn't talk like his sister does. He lives in one of those cabins down across from that, the big there, those three little ones in a row. But she recalls, she has a wonderful mind and she recalls so much. She lives and spoke to her, and she has Margaret Clover, or Margaret Wells now.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: They had at one time a store, and they were in the post office down there at... Albert Cross. Oh no.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: They owned that and then they moved their store from there up over to where the, is it Bill and I? On your folks at that time?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Well, I don't think they had an easy time of it, but I don't, they didn't complain really, I don't think. They took it just like... People in those days, I think... People nowadays don't know what hard times it are, so... Well, I mean... Of course not. I mean, they didn't have any modern conveniences or anything like that. They carried the water from the spring and things like that, but that was expected. They all did, so... If they had a horse, they had a horse transportation, if they didn't, they walked. Reuben tells about his dad going to Moscow and carrying a flower home on his back. Well, you know, and now Mom told about how she went out to begin with and picked up every loose stick for firewood. They'd been used to not having anything back there in Minnesota that way because they just don't have the forest. And she said she thought that was such terrible waste out here. She said Mrs. Grattus, she mentioned her, you know, how she did that too. Well, they'd come from Minnesota where they homesteaded back there and their families, so... I mean, it was just... Another generation doing the same thing.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you think that your folks had money to live on or when they came out here that they had saved, or do you think it was just real subsistence?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Well, I imagine they had some, you know, I don't know, just I wouldn't say how much, but...

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I can say, I've always felt that while we didn't have a great deal, we certainly were very competitive and happy, and I think we had a very happy childhood, you know, and all.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: It certainly didn't bother me. Well, tell me a little bit of what being a kid was like, what childhood was like.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Well, of course, there was a large family. There were six of us girls.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: The kids, in those days, made your own fun. In the night, in the evenings, there'd be a whole bunch of us get together and play games and things like that. And we all had our chores or certain things we had to do. We knew we had to do them. And to me, that teaches you responsibility, and I think so many children now have any responsibilities whatsoever. They don't learn to go ahead and do what they're supposed to do. And my grandfather lived with us, and he kept the wood chock. It was our job to carry the wood. Sometimes we have to carry the water, things like that, but I never thought that I was really...

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Every one of the other kids did so much and not. Many times we'd get together as a group and we'd go from one house to the other and help each other, do the load chores they had to do so we could out and play and have our games. And we could be together doing it. It was just a matter of fact. It had to be done. I believe, and lots of times, when we went home at noon, in our lunch at noon, it was our responsibility to see the table was cleared up and things like that before we went back to school at noon.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Because Mom had other things that had to be done. She had a lot to do there to keep things up for the six of us.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You knew what you had to do rather than being told by the parents?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Usually, yes. We knew that these things had to be done every day or when the time came. We knew that if we didn't get in and do them, we would have to... Later anyway, so we might as well see that they were done.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you wind up helping your father very much in the outside work at all?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: He wasn't home to do it. He worked out in the woods. He was in the office at the... We took pajamas and helped with that kind of stuff. That's all we had because we... And a little garden. We helped with that.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: So mostly he was working out in the woods.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: After a little diddare yes. He was then... To begin with, they traded the homestead to the store. He was a historical father. Not he was a realie for a while. But then he went to work in the camps and was a clerk in the camps. He was with Camp 6. That's all I remember. It was headquarters of the... I mean it was kind of headquarters for the camps there at 6. And then he went to a little boat bill and he was the opposite of a boat bill. And then when he came back it was during the Depression and he worked as a... A foreman. A CCC... No CCCCC. And then shortly after that... He was postmaster. He was a postmaster there.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: But then you worked out on Bear Creek and the logging down there?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Well for harsh. The timber. Yeah, it was in the timber but he worked on it. Logging.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well talking about the work that you kids were supposed to do, did this leave you very much free time?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Oh yes, we had plenty of free time. We played every evening if we wanted to. We were out... The whole community would get together, the kids. And we'd play games together. Run sheep, run hide and go sleep. Just games like that that we didn't have a lot of playthings. We didn't have playthings and we didn't have money to buy things. We just had fun.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What kind of spread of age would there be among the kids that would get together and play? Was it a wide age group?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Oh yeah, it's from the school.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: First grade on through. Sometimes even high school kids play together. It was when we were playing. Run sheep run that I... You know, Gories, when they came there I had met Dorothy and she got down there some way. And it was the first time I had seen Dorothy. She was in high school and she was off playing with the little kids.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How do you play run sheep run?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: It's a hide and seek game. You have two teams and one team stays at the home base. The other goes out and they have a leader that takes them out and hides them and gives them certain signals. And they're supposed to, maybe they yell red and that means they're supposed to go to a certain place and the others in the meantime are trying to find further hidden. And they have their signals to tell them to sneak from one place to another, try to get in.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: You're trying to get to home base.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Yes. Those things were really lots of fun. I think kids know. They do some of those things. Take the can, of course it was one too. Really enjoy it.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Now what about... I've heard that there were a lot of party games that were played in the schools too.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was that true around here?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Oh, yes. Not during school but in communities to get together.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: We used to have parties. School parties and have lots of fun at those too. That's right. For every basketball game we usually entertained the visiting team and had a party for them afterwards. I remember one time a sledding party where we got sleds and after the basketball game we had a party and then where we all took our sleds and went coasting. But we always entertained the visiting team after basketball. Of course at that time they used to stay overnight a lot of times and they'd stay in the homes. The players would stay in the homes of the local players or whoever had room.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Well that's kind of nice because I've heard a lot about the rivalry between the towns when they played basketball. It was really quite a...

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I don't know if that was true. Well in the game it was but that... Well they didn't have hard feelings of anyone at that time. We made good friends and some people we kept track of for years that we would stay in their homes you know when we went to Potlatch and Elk River.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Parkier?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Parkier, Fernwood. My daughter met a girl up in Elk River, from Elk River the other day and she said well, mentioned she said well you probably knew my mother. And she said well I didn't know her but I knew her older sisters. They used to play basketball and I knew them then.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What was the setup on basketball? How big were the teams?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Well we had a girls team the same as the boys and we made lots of times the very same trips that the boys did.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: We'd go to Elk River and stay overnight and play and usually just one team. We didn't have a sack of string like they do now. But we would go and make most of the trips that the boys did. One time the coach's wife decided that we couldn't... maybe the train would make connections at Bovill and they started out with a sled to take us to Bovill. We got up as far as a flag place and the team gave out and we had to walk from flags to Bovill to catch the train. We made it even though we had to walk most of the way and got on the train up there to go on to Elk River to play basketball.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Would you remember the games as being...

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: did you do a lot of practice? Was there a lot of skill involved or was it mostly fun?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Well we practiced quite a bit but not like they do today. We had the old, what they call the old Legion Hall and it was just a cracker box.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: There wasn't any room along the side. If people stood along the side they were really on the court. There was just a little stage where they could see it. But that's our practice and after they built the high school then we had to go from the Legion Hall up to the high school to shower. Sometimes by the time we got up there we were perspiring and our hair would be frozen stiff by the time we got up to the high school to shower. But we enjoyed it and it was fun. And you were not the worst for it either. No, we weren't.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: We had lots of fun. There was one team for the whole high school. Yes, one team for the whole high school. Both of the boys and girls. The boys didn't have a second string either. Well I think I better go and take care of this. Yeah, I'll be back.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: When you first moved into Deary, what was the school situation at that time? Did they didn't have the high school?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: No, just elementary school.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: When the folks first moved here, of course none of our family was yet in school when they first moved here. And then of course they built the building up, that was up there close to where the school is now. And my grandfather and uncle helped build it. And my uncle was injured. He fell for it and they said that his dad was an indirect result of the fall of the building when he was working out. Oh Lord. But that was building the second story down the building they had up there. It tells about it in those books about how they, when they decided to put a second story on and so on.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you know how he fell? What happened?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: No, he was working up on top somewhere. That's all I know about.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What did you think of Deary when you first moved in?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Well I was just six weeks, six months old when they moved here. You were just a little bit. Yeah, I was just six months old when they moved here.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: So I couldn't think about it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you remember Harsh?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Oh yes.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: He was a real, I think a real good fellow in the deal with. Now I know when we got ready to go to school the folks would go away to college. The folks couldn't afford to send us. They didn't have the money.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: And talk went down and talked to him and he said, well I've never turned your dog in, have I?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: So we got money. Then we borrowed to go to school and paid it back when we got out and started working.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I guess he has a more mixed reputation. And I think bankers, a lot of bankers will tend to have that kind of reputation because those who they supported will think a lot more highly of them than those who they did. Well I think that's maybe true too.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: And sometimes the people who maybe don't think so much of some of those people are the ones, I don't know, but maybe some of them that got money and didn't want to pay it back or maybe trying to get out of it. I don't know. There may be a reason for it. Not.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: But would you say that Mr.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Harsh was really working pretty good in the community?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I think so.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Yes, don't you lose?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I think definitely at this point. But I remember, even of course he was here, but till after we were out teaching, quite a while.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you know what happened to the bank and why it failed eventually?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Once it was at the time when somebody had been paid also, you know, when they closed all over the country. I imagine it was probably he didn't get enough of that. Just like you said, maybe there were some of those that too many of them that didn't pay up and they didn't have enough to come out of it.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I want to ask you about Joe Wells and the Wells family.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you remember them very well?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Is this being a...

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: But I don't think...

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Yes, I remember them. They were well -liked and everyone, you know, they all respected them. They were just included. You didn't think of the color of their skin at all. And I didn't. We didn't have too much. We contacted them, you know, except for the kids in school, no, Louisa Jordan and Billy were in school, Louisa Jordan school when I was in there. Of course, she finished high school. They went away the day before.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I don't remember, or was she in Beverly's class?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I don't remember. I remember going up there to, I don't know, meeting campfire girls or something up there, up to their home, things like that, up to Mary's. And Billy, I remember one time in school, one of the employees just thought Billy was wonderful and he packed him around on his back all the time.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: And one day he'd been packed him around and Billy came up to me and he says, they say I'm a nigger and I'm not, am I?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: But he just felt that he was just accepted that way, you know, and he was. They weren't treated any differently.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Well, I don't know, to me, they're one of the most interesting families that I've heard about.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: And there's so much race prejudice. I mean, it's so much part of American history that to see how, and there also are not very many Negro pioneers in the West. So there are not too many out here. So to see how they were accepted is really, and what they were like as people are really important to us. Well, you think that they were brought out here by their white masters, you know, that they got enough of them to bring them out and set them up out here too.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: You know that they were pretty well thought of.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Don't you have that, or others that you've talked to about Welles' time? Isn't that the general feeling? That they were accepted?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Yes, very well accepted. And very well followed by all the people.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: It doesn't stop there from being some racial jokes. Well, that's true. You don't.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: No matter what nationality you are, or what country your ancestors are from, why they, and jokes about them. And like I say to me, it's just like that. They have the Negroes. I think it's just the ones that are trying to stir up that trouble. But, you know, like little Black Samuels, I feel a little sorry. But you aren't supposed to read tickets in school or anything like that because racial.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Stary times. Yes.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: But now they have, look at Heidi, that's a story of a little Swiss girl. And that is a wonderful story. And to me it's the same thing. Little Black Samuels, little boy. There wasn't anything wrong with him or anything like that.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: That's still, why shouldn't children hear that story?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I think maybe that story had connotations from the South. Well, probably. That are what people, some people think of it that way, and not as a kid's story. But I see what you're saying.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What was, what do you remember Mary being like, the kind of person she was?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Well, to me, she was very, very hardworking. And she used to, she used to do things, that kind of thing, for the folks. And she was working in Washington, irony. And to me, she seemed, she was always very kind.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: She was a person that I think everybody liked, really, and ill.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: But Joe, Joe, was. Roy.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Roy.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was this Chuck and Roy were the brothers?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Yes.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: And then. Joe was the father. The father, yes.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: And they worked all together, you know. They lived there. It's a great big old house.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: One of the biggest, doesn't it seem like one of the world's largest?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Yes, it did. It's that time that seemed one of the biggest houses in the country. They're on a hill.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Have you heard about the starting of the school, why they called it the Wells School?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: No, my own. I imagine. See, up there, I close to the Wells Place. Yes. It was on their land, I imagine, because Mary lived in the schoolhouse after it was, um, after they built the new school, I should move in the old schoolhouse and meet there.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I hear a lot about Joe and the boys drinking. And I sometimes wonder if it's exaggerated or if we really, you know, wore his hard drinkliness as some people tell you. I don't know any about that.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I can't remember. Of course. We weren't around, you know, around them enough that we would really know. They were, the boys were up there on the farm most of the time, I guess, and that I wouldn't know.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you think the local people ever would defend them against, you know, prejudice from the outside?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: You know, people elsewhere who don't know them and saying...

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I think the old timers, the ones that were around here at that time especially, would. I don't know about the present day people, but I think the ones that were here at that time would have.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Don't you, Lou?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Well, it seems to me like they would because they certainly were well thought of.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Mary lived out of her life here. No.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: She went to Pullman, didn't she?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I think so. I think she went over there and started working at the college or something. I wouldn't say that as a fact, but I believe that's where she was. Some of those people, what, Helmer would certainly know. I don't know why I say Helmer.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: What is there, there was a relationship there with this store at Helmer.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Now, who ran that? Weren't there a black person in the store there at Helmer?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Mildred.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Who was Chuck's wife? Wasn't that it?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Yes, Mildred and Chuck.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How did Dan Ross get married?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Well, Dan was married to Mildred.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: That was after she and Chuck? Who was Dan Ross? Was he a local?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: He was raised up by Helmer.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Where?

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was she there?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I mean, quite a family. The Rosses up there, going down.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was she there at Helmer for a long time, very long after she and Chuck split up?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Quite a while.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Until her death, I guess, she was there. I don't know how many years ago Mildred died.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: She wasn't local, right? She was from somewhere?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Yes, she was from someplace else. I don't know why.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I imagine that must have raised some eyebrows. It could even today.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Well, I guess, to be in with, maybe in some cases it did. But, I think it was just... Accepted.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: It's funny, because I had heard about there being a Negro woman at that store, and I didn't. I never thought to ask anyone.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Who?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Most of the time they were up there, that was after we were away teaching or at school or something. We weren't around here too much during those years.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you remember the fire in Deary very well, the bad one in 1923?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I think that was the year. It was the most serious of the past. Yes, we were in 1923.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I remember we woke up in the middle of the night and we saw the flames. About that time the fire was at the hardware store. Of course, they carried ammunition and all that kind of stuff there. Things started popping. The first thing I thought of, a good friend of mine was staying down there with her uncle in hand.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I was really concerned if she was out on the ride.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: It just burned. I remember standing in the window at home and watching it.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I understand that there just wasn't much water in the town. They didn't have a system.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: They used to have a town well down back in City Hall now, and many people carried water from down there.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I was reading and looking through some of the very old Deary papers. In the University Library on Microfilm, they have them. In 1908, the editor, Jason Peterson, was calling for getting a water system because of the fire danger in the town. That was 1908.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: He was talking about it way back then, isn't it?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: His son lives in Spokane, I guess, Paul Astility.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What was Martin up there, too?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I worked for him when I was in high school, Saturdays and after school. I sent out all the type by hand and distributed it all by hand with a little local paper.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Frank Davis ran the light plant in the vegetable light plant, and Frank Davis ran that. He was turned off at ten o 'clock at night, no lights after ten o 'clock.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Will you pay for doing that work for the newspaper?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Twenty -five cents an hour.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Then I worked all day Saturday, eight hours per dollar.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Even after school, I got twenty -five cents an hour.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you actually set the type yourself?

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was that paper a going concern? Did he have other work besides that?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: He didn't have other work, but he lived on a shoestring, I think. I don't think he made enough to really make what you were saying. He had as much as a lot of them.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Yes, that's right. People were satisfied with last then. I've heard in red elsewhere how the early day newspapers in a small town really were just a kind of marginal affair.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: His ads in the paper. I was trying to find a couple of the high school annuals to show you. Maybe one of them is in here. To show you the number of businesses, in theory, at one time, is really surprising. They had a shoemaker, and they had a music house or a store. It's really surprising, the number of businesses.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Have you ever seen one of those annuals?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: No. I found one of them in there, but that is the most interesting one. Of course, he got some legal notices. I remember that was one thing we had to be very careful about, these legal notices. They were set in some tiny, fine type that took forever to get anything done.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: They were set in different types. I've heard that was really important.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Those legal notices were of kind of steady income, right?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: That's right. They were always sure of that.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: He did have some of those.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: When I was playing basketball, then I'd go down and work before school in the morning so I could practice basketball after school. I'd get up and go down. My hour was so before school. The telephone company. That was owned by Bill Smith at that time. Highway garage.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Now, he printed those down there, didn't he?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Hmm.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Quite a few.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Surprising, you know.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Quite a few.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Wow. Let's see, this one. Yes, that was Deary's first basketball team. I took it down to show Russell Foster. Some of the kids came in while I had it there, and they thought that was something. They had five. That's all they had on the team, the five players.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Well, there were more girls. Yes, there were more boys.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Well, I'd like to know some of what it was like, what kind of activities there were in Deary when you were just teenagers growing up.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: What there was to do in a small town in those days. There weren't many things. Like we said, we made our own entertainment. We went out with late games. We had coasting parties. We had home parties, you know. Or maybe a party at the schoolhouse during school term. But they didn't have to have somebody entertaining all the time.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: It wasn't much organized.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: No. Other than, you know, like she said, in the schools, they had parties. And in the homes. So many of the parents, I know they'd say, well, they'd rather have a party in the home and know where their kids were than to have them out someplace and not know where they were. So maybe one week they'd have a party at one person's home, and maybe the next week somebody else's.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Would it be dancing?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Or games.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: More games, I think, than dancing. More party games.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What kind of party games are you thinking?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Oh, Skip to Maloon. Well, it's practically the same as square dancing. But at that time, they called it. I know the first time I, my folks didn't approve of dancing, and I went out to Texas Ridge to a country school. I had a very good friend there, and I used to go out and spend the weekend with her. And we went down to the schoolhouse, and, well, they played Skip to Maloon. I can't remember all of them, but they were practically the same as the square dances. And I came back, and I told Mom that they played those games out there. And, of course, that was just about wrong, I guess. I don't know. Because it was so much like dancing. But, you know, the way I can't remember.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You know where I went?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: That was one game. Well, you'd stand, you'd sit in a chair, chairs in a circle, and the girls would sit in the chairs, and the boys would stand back with them. And if there was always one more in the chairs, no. One less in the chairs. The one standing in front. And the one that didn't have a partner, someone in their chair, they'd wink at one of the others. And then they were supposed to try to get away and get over in that chair. But if their partner put their hands on their shoulder, they had to stay there. That was one hand. But some of the others, I can't remember, but two.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Why were you both supposed to dance?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Well, I don't know. A lot of them, I think, were in their daycare. I've heard it before. I wonder why. I figured that they must have thought it wasn't moral for some reason.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I don't know. A lot of them were. And later the folks weren't. We went to the school dances, and we went to Grange all the time. And they went, and they danced after Grange meetings and things like that. But at one time they weren't.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Your parents themselves danced?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: No, they'd ever dance, I don't think. I don't remember if his brothers did. Not one. And Hank did, too.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I don't think the Lutheran Church, I mean, when they were in the East, they belonged to the Lutheran Church.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I don't believe that they believed too much in dancing, did they?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I think perhaps not.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I think that Scarlow and Mom, of course, was... Wasn't a lot of very...

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How did it happen that you both decided that you wanted to teach?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Well, you know, at that time there weren't many... You know, openings for women, for girls, you know, to get out. My oldest sister was a nurse, in fact, last Thursday, or last Saturday. They had their class reunion in Spokane. She graduated from the Deaconess Hospital fifty years ago. And we had to stop there and sing and spend several days with her. And she'd been up in Spokane, there were seven of her class in the Deaconess. To the dinner, the band went the night before, and she said, yeah, great time. But now, nursing and teaching, and some did office work, but I always... To me, I always thought I wanted to teach. I liked children, and I always thought I liked them.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you get that idea when you were going to school, and did you have it for a long time at elementary school or in that school?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Well, I think the teachers play a lot. They've acquired a lot of what you want. I had some teachers that I thought an awful lot of, and I really admired them. And I think that's one thing. And of course, my grandfather was the teacher and my mother was the teacher. And like I said, some of the teachers that I had, I certainly had muttered and I found a lot of. And I think that's partly why I went that way.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How about you?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Well, it's partly the same thing, and I was interested a lot in home economics. But I went up and started working with that, and at the time, couldn't go on to finish. I had to finish two years and go out and work, so I'd go on to school. And by the time I got to where I was able to go on and finish up, I decided that I didn't want to work with the older ones after seeing and working with the younger ones. And some of the problems with coming from the older ones, I decided I'd rather stay with them at the lower level. So I just stayed in elementary. Well, I have to ask you what you saw as the problems in those days with the older kids. Some of the discipline problems and things that they were encountering with some of the older ones. Well, and they were so much minor compared to the younger days. Yes, and they were minor. Like I said, some of the kids that I had in school now, or at a school when I was teaching, and I thought they were kind of problems to a certain extent, and troublemakers, there wouldn't be anything compared to things that I saw in the last few years that I taught.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Well, Tim, then give me an idea of what discipline problems would have been in those days. What you saw as problems.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: So I can get an idea of the difference between them now. They wouldn't be considered problems at all now. Just somehow maybe rebelling a little bit about some of the things that maybe you asked them to do. Just objecting and these kind of things where they didn't want to get work to work and do what you're asking them to do. And it wouldn't be anything today.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: When you see some of the things now, and every time that you try to, therefore, the last few years you try to get some of them to do something, but you make me do this or you do that, my folks are going to sue you. And this kind of thing. The thing that is coming up now all the time. We saw it too much the last few years we were teaching.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Where do you think you got the interest in home economics from?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Probably from my mother. She helped us a lot. She helped us with cooking. She helped us with sewing. And this kind of thing. And that's the kind of thing I like to do and do with her. Now, some of the family weren't as much interested in that kind of thing. They'd like to go outside and work in the yard and do things like that more.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you go to Moscow?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: No. My first college was at Cheney. I didn't go to Moscow at all. My college was outside of... Well, I went to Lewiston one summer, otherwise it was all in the by -the -home.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: But it was financial reasons that made you decide to start teaching. Yes, I finished two years and then went out to teach, to begin with.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: And then you went to school? And then you went to school? Where did you go to school?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I did most of my work at Cheney too.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How did you happen to go to Cheney?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Well, I had a cousin that went there. I had a couple cousins that went there. And they liked it so much that I think that was partly what influenced us. Or in a way too, I kind of... This older sister was in Spokane at the time, training. And I thought, well, I'd get there and be close to Winterbread. And I used to spend a lot of weekends in Spokane with her at the hospital. And Cheney was considered a very good school at that time. I think it was rated higher than Lewiston. And that, of course, is Cheney and Lewiston were the two for training, teachers. Teachers training colleges, they called them at that time. And I think Cheney had a better... It was rate higher than Lewiston. I had several quarters of Lewiston at summer school there. We went to Montana, right to Bellingham.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Can you tell me a little about what college life was like then?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I've read about the 20s as being the flapper age. It was more collegiate maybe than it had been before. Maybe it wasn't that way at Cheney, but I was just curious about that.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What would you say?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Well, I was a flapper age, all right. I can't see as... There's much difference than it was any other age. Those days, though, there were no cars on campus. If anybody had a car, they were just... They left it at home. Well, I know that when we were up there... One time when we were there, a bunch of us decided we wanted to come... The folks were living at Bolell and we decided we wanted to come home with a friend. Well, they wanted to come down with us and they borrowed a car. Just wanted to borrow the car.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How many six of us?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Six of us. It was very seldom that anyone had a car at that time around the campus at all.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I know when we were at Lewiston, in a lot of ways, you've been to the school there, haven't you? Where is it?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: If we wanted to go downtown, the only way to get there was to walk. We'd walk downtown, shop, go back up to the school, we looked at the dorms.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: And even in those schools, there wasn't too much social activity. There was absolutely no smoking allowed in the dorms at all. I remember we went into a friend's room one evening and she was all panicky. We had a house meeting and the house mother announced that there was no smoking and she did smoke. She had quite a few cigarettes there. She was getting them wrapped up in a hurry so she could send them home the next day to get them out of her room because she's afraid she'd be kicked out of school if they were found there.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: She was hustling around, get those things hidden.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Where was she?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: She was from Montana. She didn't stay very too long. She just stayed the first year I was there. I don't think you knew her.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Were there any men at the school going to school for teacher training too?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Oh yes. They had one dorm, all men in the dorm.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: But still, it seemed to me like a great majority of the teachers would win. Oh, that's true.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: There was a great percentage of women there. I can't even remember where they lived it. The Louis Hall.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I want to ask you this.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you feel at all at the time that there was a concern about a lack of opportunity for women?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: You know, I've always, of course, talked about racial prejudice there, you know, and discrimination. But I can't. It's true that men, of course, a little later when they had so much activity in athletics, the men would get their salary from teaching. Then they also got a salary for coaching and that. And they got higher salaries than women.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You look at that book there, those books there, and it shows there isn't too much discrimination, is there?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: It gives the salary of the men and women in the school. And I can't see where the women were discriminating against too much.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I think that what strikes me is the fact that almost all women had to go if they wanted a career into either teaching or nursing.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: It was limited at that time. It's definitely true. Now, if I'd have lived, I don't know how many years later, I certainly would have gone into forestry or something like that. But at that time, that would be unthinkable. I'd work for the Forest Service and all the work out and that kind of stuff, and I'd really enjoy that kind of stuff. But at that time, I was doing my own work. I didn't think a woman was crazy to go into that field.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I think that's what I mean. Looking back at it, that seems like a narrow view of what women could do.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Well, of course, a lot of them didn't expect to go out. A lot of them expected to marry and go in, and they didn't expect to go out and work after they were married. They expected to stay home and take care of their home and their family. And there weren't so many going out looking for jobs.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Well, that's another thing. It strikes me that it seems like most women who were married, say they'd talked for a few years, they got married, then they always seemed to stop teaching. Now, was that...

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you know whether that was what they had to do or whether most of them just wanted to stop teaching?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Those women hire a married teacher.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: That's true. And if they were married, then their job was over.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: But what's the...

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What would the reason for that be?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: That they wouldn't want to... That they would... I mean, there's no...

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I just can't see why that would happen. Well, I think that maybe it was because there weren't too many openings, and they felt that this other woman had a man to take care of and find the livelihood. And it wasn't necessarily a good job. Now, I know a lot of... Some of the friends, you know, they said that they were married, but they kept it a secret for her until school was out because they wanted to finish teaching. And it happened quite often. They knew that... The school board knew that they were married when they'd be out. I guess a contract wasn't... I don't know, maybe the contract stated that. It may have, I don't know.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Of course, that might or might not be true, that I would think that... I mean, I imagine in some cases a family would be struggling, could be very much struggling with just one member of the family working. I mean, the reason that... One of the main reasons why both... Why spouses were...

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Both of them worked these days is because it takes two, you know?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: They didn't demand... I mean, they didn't expect to find those days. They didn't have to have everything. I know one year when I was... The year I went to Colfax to teach, our principal was really put out. He says... Some of these younger folks coming in wanting jobs, and then he says they'd call him as a principal and ask him if he could find them an apartment or help him find an apartment. And he says they won't have anything but the best. He says, Thelma and I... But he's still... They were still using a wood stove. He says we're satisfied with that, but he says these new ones coming out won't have anything but electric range and everything. The best of everything.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Would this have been in the 50s maybe?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Yeah, about 50s or late 40s.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Yeah, so then you're saying expectations really changed. That's right. When I think about it then, it seems like a person would be forced to make a choice if you were woman teaching between family and career to some extent if you wanted to teach. That's right. They would.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Which is a choice that men certainly didn't have to make at all. No.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: No.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: When you first taught, where were you teaching?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: My first year was in a rural school out here, so it was still... The building is still standing out here, south of the dairy.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What was it? The name of this?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: The Applequist. Applequist, I've heard of that.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you know where Alvin Nelson is?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: No, I don't think I do. I was just across from the house that he's living in. I batched in this whole farmhouse that he's living in now.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: That was my first school.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Who was it like to teach you?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Well... You raised the water, built the fires, swept the floors. That was part of your work along with teaching. You were janitor too. No lights.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: And sometimes, I think, they were a whole lot better than they are today. The sanitation, you know, everything else was supposed to be so sanitary and everything like that. And here they'd have an old water bucket and a back of the school. Sometimes they had a different hang there, but sometimes we had... They had their tin cups, you know. But we drank out the same different... And they lived too.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Did you feel that you could... Where was your...

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Mine was out here too. I taught... It's on Texas Ridge at the Elwood School. It's still standing there. It was a two -room school. It was a two -room school. I had the first four grades of Mr. Barrett. His son lives in Monteskull now, but Mr. Barrett taught me other grades.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: That sounds a little luxurious to have two rooms there for the school instead of two teachers.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was it because there were a lot of kids?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: There was a lot, yes, for that to... Well, the farms were so much more than they are now, out there on the ridge. And, you know, houses... Well, we'll say, well, we'd wrap along there with some of these grants. Well, this was where Albert Beersons used to be. This is where Bob Adcock's place used to be. This is where Queens and Berry's house used to be. And you can... Place after place, the house is gone. And at that time, of course, there were families living there with three, four, five children in the family. So there weren't quite a few, just a lot of people that we know who did this ridge at that time.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you feel that you could take care of all of the needs of the kids and the way of learning at that time? Or with having to teach so many grades, was it really difficult?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: It was difficult, but children learned... I mean... They learned from each other a lot. Yes, they did. Those younger children would listen to the older ones. Our school day was longer than it is today, too. We never let out before four o 'clock at night. And some of those kids, you know, from those rural schools, would come into high school and do fine, you know, do as well. And I felt better than some of those living in town. Of course, now I have a little place like this to have the range of... Or the fields that they can go into. But those out there in those rural schools, they came in and I think they were... That's ready for their high school and their college, just a lot of the others. You can look back at some of the, you know, that have gone on and... Well, there's one little boy that under him died.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: School was a pleasant hill. It was down between here and Troy. And he was a very bright, a bright child. And I think I had him three years in that school. And he went on to high school, and of course when he got into high school, he was just tall. He had the ability to do it. And he went on to college. He's a doctor now. Look at that year that that report was in the paper from Moscow. They had the averages from the schools throughout the state. Elk River had the top average of high school students at the University of Idaho, and Deary had the third ranking. All of that in these small high schools. And those kids were mostly kids that had come in from rural schools and gone to high school.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Well, is what...

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Thinking that it was better, actually?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Well, I don't say it was better, but I think at that time I think you were doing just as good a job for the children in their rural schools as they were in town. They just had the fundamentals. I mean, like you might say, the reading, writing, and that particular thing like that. Of course we went into social studies and that.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: But... They didn't expect all this extra stuff that they expect nowadays.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: And I don't think some of it's necessary.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Extra stuff like what?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Like band and that sort of thing. Well, bands are alright for kids after they get up a ways, but I think sometimes they start that too.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Hey, there are kids in the car up to a meeting place so they can go on a hike.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Why couldn't the kid hike up there?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: When you think of the distance those kids in the country had to walk to a school, it wasn't good. I mean, it was hard, I'm sure, but they certainly survived and they didn't seem to hurt many. One thing that I know we kind of... When we were over there at Moses Lake, they kind of had one of them and they got the idea that whenever we took the children out for recess, they should have a supervised game. That they should be playing all the same thing. And we said no, we thought that they needed to get out there and have some freedom of their own where they decided what they were going to do. We'd be there to supervise so they didn't get hurt or get into trouble in this kind of thing, but we didn't think it should be supervised play. And I think they need more of this, where they're on their own to do the kind of activities they want to do.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, do you think that kind of means that there's too much organization that goes on now or too much expecting all the kids to do the same thing? In the form?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I think that area especially. Yes. In what's supposed to be their free time especially, I think. I think they should be... And like I say, we objected to that until finally. We weren't required to do it anymore because we finally made them see that we felt it. And they didn't need that super... or that organized play. We needed to be there as supervisors.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Okay, is Janice a 3, 4, 4, 5?

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you do most of your teaching around here?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Yes. No.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I taught in rural schools here for several years now, was it Colfax for 11 years and Moses Lake for 16 years?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Okay, then.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What did you teach mostly?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Intermediate grades.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Okay, I was looking around this morning...

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You were saying you taught at Park?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Yes.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What was that like? Did you find Park?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I enjoyed it out there. I really did. It was Park's just a little community that's old and they made their own entertainment. We didn't have cars so we'd get in and out whenever we wanted to go. We went in there and stayed. If we went out in the wintertime, we went out with a sled and a team. You know, you would understand a child. You would understand when you lived in a community like that. You could understand children a lot more. A lot better. Well, I know I had one little girl. She would just use swear words all the time constantly. When I got to know her parents, I knew why, because that was part of their conversation.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Why?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I mean, it wasn't a child's fault. That's all she heard at home. She accepted that as a way to talk. One time I said, Betty, I said, let's be careful. I tried to talk to her and tell her how to talk. I said, we don't talk like that.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: She said, why don't you?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: You really got to understand a child. You could see that a lot of their problems were caused right at home.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I enjoyed it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you feel there was much chance to help children with their problems?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Well, some you could. There wasn't too much.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: That was just their way of life.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I just was thinking more what teachers in those days would feel they were responsible to do. If you could make a neat division between studies and personal things, or if you kind of had to deal with both.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Well, you have to deal with both. You have to deal with both, trying to get them to see their responsibilities in studying and then in their behavior. I have to get this done.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: It all works together, just like I think that a teacher, you have your guidance people in your schools and everything like that, but I think a teacher has more effect, or can work better in guiding a child. These people come in and try to, our psychologists and all that. You have more influence on them. You're with them every day.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you feel like you got to know the kids really well?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Oh, yes. You know, in the hot news. In those communities, especially in those rooms, usually I think you were invited into their homes.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: You were in their homes. You saw how they lived. You knew the children so much better than me. Nowadays.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you think that the kids in those communities, were they, I know this is a hard thing to know, but were they individualists? Do they stand out as individuals?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I often get the feeling that kids today tend to be more of a, I don't know, I don't have a very long time span to look at it only in 25 years. It seems like there's a lot of similarities, kids, one kid to another. This is a, well, I don't know.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I think that kids, to a certain extent, were individuals, but then too, when you think about these little communities, they all were together so much all the time that they just, but they seem to get along most of the time. They seem to not have any difficulties. When I retired, they had written, this was just showing what impressed a child in those days. This, the one that wrote this letter, she is a teacher in Spokane, and I had her in a rural schools up by Priest River. And it says, thank you for spending some of your teaching time at Meagan School in Idaho. I'm so glad I was privileged to have you as my fifth grade teacher. As I look back on that year, I find I had many memories, and they're happy ones indeed. The Christmas programs we had in the Grange Hall, the delicious soup and spaghetti you fixed on the big wood stove for our hot lunch, the walks we took looking for wildflowers, the baseball games. I was hit square in the eye with a fast one. The library furniture we made from orange crates and apple boxes, they were beautiful, painted orange and blue, the walks to school with the Hirst, the Harold and the Hirst children, and that kindness you showed me that I had such a terrible society. Anything like that. But not like that. You knew the child, and you thought of them and tried to work with them and do for them.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: We used to, Friday afternoon, I can remember down at Pleasant Hill, not on that school down there by, between here and Troy. That was after recess on Friday. We had kind of a crafts time. We had coping saws and things like that, and then cut out old magazine racks, and we painted with crayons and things like that, and sent it to the county fair. That was a big time for them. It took so little at that time, just like this, to make an impression on them. We have so much in our lives today, and kids have so many things to play with, but these little things like making furniture out of a crate, to them, to Donna, that meant a lot. Today, they have too much. But still, a lot of children love to learn and work with their hands. They don't do it too much anymore, I think.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Those are really simple things that she's talking about today. That's right, and it impressed her so much.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you think that the teacher had a special role in the community, in the community's life?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Definitely.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: A teacher was one of the most respected people in the, don't you think so?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I think so. They've come to you for so many things, you know.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: There's an old man, he was eighty -seven years old, and they used to have parties at the school every once in a while. If a child had a birthday, they'd bring a cake and a lot of community would come up there. This day Mr.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Chamberlain came up to me and he says, how many pay -per - equals do we want to wear nowadays?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I said, well, I used to be wear just one. He says, that's what I told Lettie, that she was bound with a long three today.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: You were asked a question, I knew what that would be.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: You were asked about the way things should be done.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: And it was - Etiquette. They thought, they considered the teacher quite an authority. Another thing that always, I was playing that, this one mother told me, she says, Sue and John Rowan from Farture one day, and she said she was in the living room. And the door was open and she heard them talking, and they were talking about people. Sue said, well, mother is smart, and John says yes, but she isn't as smart as Ms. Olsen. Ms. Olsen knows almost as much as God. But that was her idea, you could answer their simple questions, and that's the way they felt. You could answer their questions, and their questions usually were simple ones.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: And you had an answer for them, why?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: But some day, even now, I taught first grade for so many years, even in the first grade, a lot of times they felt that the teacher knows very much. You can't pull them very often, like I had John food.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Would you be asked for a buy?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: One ex -teacher told me that she would actually send for information on things that local people wanted to know about, things that she couldn't answer.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you ever have that kind of experience of being asked for technical advice?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: This was, I think, digging, well digging.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I don't know if we've ever done, but I remember ever doing that, but lots of times we've referred them to places where they could send for information, where they come and want information on something, and maybe you couldn't, and maybe you'd refer them to some. I don't remember ever having sent for it. Well, now I can.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Over there at Moses Lake, I know one time, one of the mothers came to school, and I had, well, Margaret had started getting the Ranger Rick for her room at school. It's surprising how much money you spend in your school room for the kids, your salary. Margaret had ordered Ranger Rick, and her kids had enjoyed it, the little folks. I had copies of Ranger Rick at school. I subscribed for it. A mother came to school, and her son had been telling things that we'd been talking about, you know, nature. I showed her this Ranger Rick, and I said, if you want to get something for him, the boy was a very bright boy, and he was definitely interested in that kind of stuff. I think one of the nicest things she would get for Christmas would be a subscription of Ranger Rick. So she did. One of the first things that they saw when they got the magazine was something about the submarines when they were down under the ice up north, you know. It happened to be that one of the fellows in the submarine that was telling this story was Dick had known him. He worked with him. Much of the little boy came to school and said that that man, that story was a friend of his dad's, but they do books and things like that. They often ask for information, what to get for a child. That was interesting, their interest in a book that would fit the need.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I had, you know, Bobby Nelson in my room, and his brother was in the front of the submarine. He took a day off from school to go over and meet him when he came in and over to Seattle.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was there any special kind of books that you found really especially nice to read to the kids in your teaching, things that you thought were really spoke to them?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Well, I think it varied according to your class and the interests. I think one group could read one thing and one another, but there were books that, oh, I can't recall what ones are now in particular, but one year I read that, and maybe two or three years later I thought, well, that would fit this class and use the same book. But this is one thing I think that definitely they need is some book that you're reading to them because it carries along and keeps them going along through the year, and it's something that they enjoy.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What did you say keeps them going along? You mean they wait for the next chapter?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I remember feeling that way when I was in school.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Sometimes they love, why did you have to stop right there?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: You stopped right there on purpose.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you do much for teaching here, dear?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: You taught around. We taught in some, we taught, let's see, I was in Idaho 18 years in Washington, 25, I guess. So I was in Washington most of the time.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was there any particular reason why you both found better teaching over there than here?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Well, I went there about the time of the war. Well, the salary's a bit much better. I was in Plummer and just across the line they called me and asked me if I'd be interested in coming to Fairfield, and the salary was so much better. That's probably what you teach, you know. Then, too, if I'd gone back to Plummer, they'd want me to take over as great as the principal. I knew there were some problems coming up, but I didn't want to do that.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you see much consolidation going on when you were teaching?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Well, most of the schools we went into were pretty well consolidated already. That is the ones that weren't consolidated. Of course, to begin with, here we were in rural schools, and they later came in here, but we were away from here at the time they came in. These are the range Rick and I was talking about. It's a nature magazine, and I've always been kind of a theme for nature. I like that. Steele and Taney and Rimrock and Fern Hill and Applequist and Elwood, Buckhorn, Liberty, all out south of town here. Well, in between here and Troy, there was Brannon and Pleasant Hill and Spring Valley, just right along.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Well, there's Bear Creek. Oh, Bear Creek, yes. Right between here and Troy. Quite close to the highway, too.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: These ones that you listed are all on Texas Ridge and Ellis Bear Ridge.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you think there was a wide variation in these little schools in terms of the size of the attendance, the number of kids that were going in the teaching?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Oh, I think there was.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I think some of them were always quite a bit smaller than others.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, Liberty was always a one -room school, wasn't it?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Buckhorn and Elwood were two -room schools. The old Steele school is what is now the dining room down at Grange Hall. Well, in the Buckhorn school is the house up here that our top corridor is in. That was brought in and they made into a house.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I was going to ask you about the depression and what effect that had around people on yourselves.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Oh, we just plain didn't have much. There were times when you didn't have anything for money to buy anything. I know one day it was after the banks closed and we had our warrants. We got warrants in from school then for teaching. We had those and the dairy bank had closed. We had, of course, some money in the dairy bank. That was a great deal. But we had our warrants. We had a checking count of dairy. But no cash and we couldn't get any. My dad, we wanted to buy a tire. I guess we had to fly a tire on the way to Moscow or someplace. We wanted to buy it on that Troy when we came through. We didn't have any cash or anything like that. I imagine if we had gone to Homerdance, we had a service station there. We could have gotten easy enough. We didn't want to. We wanted to pay for it. Pop says, well, just a minute. He says, I'm going in to see Holy Bowman, Holy Bowman. He went and told them that we had these warrants.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I guess we had a couple of them didn't we?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: We had to middle the cash and we needed some money. Only says, well, he says, I can't let them have all the cash. He says, if they'll start checking, come here. He says, they can write checks when they want to get money that way. That's when we started making it Troy.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: It was just tight at every place. We couldn't pay our board and room. We were boarding and rooming out. The schools were teaching. We couldn't pay them. We didn't have anything to pay it with.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Because you weren't being paid for teaching?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: We were getting warrants, but they weren't taking them any place until the bank opened again. We couldn't get any cash. Many of the times our warrants were registered. We had to get a bank that would take them and hold them. We had to hold them until they were called because there weren't funds in the district funds to pay them.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Where were you teaching at that time?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I was out park at the time. I mentioned I was at Pleasant Hill.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Both in the area.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you see its effects on the communities that you were teaching? Did it cause them much of a change?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I don't think it was a great big change. I think they just made the best out of it.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: The school was a center of the community and everything. Their parties, their social life, everything sort of revolved around that. Of course they had their church meetings and their ladies saying that. But of course we were teaching. We couldn't go to those.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: They found their social life in the community. They didn't have to go out for entertainment or anything like that. Some people wouldn't have called it much entertainment. We've said so often the way people go nowadays. I remember that I had been down to Kendrick Gray twice when I graduated from high school. We went down to Kendrick once to play basketball. They took us down in the back of a truck. Once we went to Lewiston to have our graduation pictures taken.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I don't think much more than that to Moscow.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: The school was generally really the social center of the small communities.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: You hear so many of them say when they took the school away, they took everything away from the community. They didn't have any gathering place or anything. There were so many of them in the schools that spent the buildings maintained or didn't care often. They eventually turned out and moved out.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I've heard that said even in big communities like Biola, which lost its foot to Moscow, that it just changed.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was it still highly important in a town like Deary? Did it still have the same important role? Was it considerably less important because of the other things?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I think it was pretty important.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Maybe not quite as much, but I think the schools were the center. Everybody was interested in the schools and what was going on there and helping them.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I'm not going to stay much longer. I just want to ask you a little bit more about Deary in the 20s.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: It seems so different to me. These small towns like Deary and Genesee, Elke River, and the other one, they lost the mill.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: To look at this kind of thing and see all the businesses and all that that was going on, was it pretty much self -sufficient? In terms of for your needs, the family shopping and all that kind of thing?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: They had to be. They didn't have any way to get out to shop.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you use Sears and Roebuck much?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: That was, well of course, Deary at one time, they had stores where they carried dry goods a lot more than materials for sewing in that.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Curtis had a real nice hardware store here. I think transportation has changed everything. Easy to have to taste. It's so easy to get out and get things other places. Like we say, just like what's happened to Bovill there, without a store, they just have that little place now where they can go and get the bread and milk and a few things like that. It's going to be a hardship on some of those people because I know quite a few of them that have transportation. Now are they going to get more of the staples than that, I haven't been in that place up there, but they say they carried just a few things to the particles.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Have you been in there?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Yeah, I have been in there a couple years. Well of course they just changed, they lost their store this spring. Oh, then I don't know about that. No. Well see, their store is gone and in the back of a tavern, they have one room there. Oh, I didn't know that. When they can get milk and bread and things like that. Oh, that's a shame. It is. That's all they have. And when you, like we were over to, they called and wanted to come over to that, what was that meeting that comes when aging, when they were talking about this bus. They said they had money in the district to buy a bus and we went over and when we got there we saw it was all from Moscow and we told them. They had a bus. They are the ones that needed more than these people so they can get to entertainment. Those people needed because of necessity. At the meeting, so many of the Moscow people said, well they thought it would be wonderful if they would get a bus so they could attend these night entertainments, the university and things like that. That's where their interest was. And one woman said that when they had that bus, that trial bus there, she rode downtown every day. Well, I don't think that was really necessary. But to people like both, the animal bill there and there are taxpayers within the county and support it. They are entitled or something to and even if they had a bus once a week or twice a week so they could get out because before long they aren't going to be able to get the perished vegetables and things like that. Oh yes. Well if they could have both and so on, that entertainment and so on is fine. But I think some of these necessities, those people out there are bad.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Like we said, we grow. We have our own transportation as far as we are concerned if we want to get some place bad enough we go. But some of these people, they don't drive, they don't have transportation. And one time they brought them back on that bus from Moscow to Deary and I had gone down there to meet one of them that I knew was coming back to take something down for. And several from Bovill came down and the one who was supposed to come back to get them, they had to get their own transportation as far and back. They weren't there. They were stranded.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How were they going to get back to Bovill?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: I said, well, we'd take them up. So we took them up. They are just in bad need up there for something.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: No, I think you have no question about that. I felt that way for a long time about the need for transportation in the county. But Moscow has a population and they seem to have the clout.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: That's right.

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: Well, I'll get going. Let's get on towards 12. Almost 10 to. One more thing. They used to have revivals around here.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What do you remember?

speaker: Ruth or Margaret Olson
words: This was just funny. It was in the times when the times were hard. There was a couple of us. A young man and his sister, if I remember this one, if I remember. And it really got pretty hot. So in this past election later on, Tom took out his purse and everything he had in was a dollar. And that was a lot of money then, you know. And so he put that in. He was so mad at me, she says, well, of course, to them, having that dollar so they could go to a dance was more important than that. The way you did this collection plate for the revival meeting. I can always remember how disgusted little was at Tom for putting that darn bill in the collection plate. This revival meeting.
